history.q: Which Danish king boasted on a runestone at Jelling that he "made the Danes Christian"?
history.fact: Harald's great Jelling stone, raised around 965, is often called Denmark's birth certificate.

history.q: Which Danish king ruled England, Denmark and Norway in the early 11th century?
history.fact: Cnut's "North Sea Empire" did not outlast his sons, and his remains lie in Winchester Cathedral in England.

history.q: Which country occupied Denmark from April 1940 to May 1945?
history.fact: The Danish government stayed in office until August 1943, when it resigned rather than accept new German demands.

history.q: Which Danish queen brought Denmark, Norway and Sweden together in the Kalmar Union of 1397?
history.fact: Margaret had her young grand-nephew, Eric of Pomerania, crowned king of all three realms at Kalmar.

history.q: Which British admiral is said to have put a telescope to his blind eye at the Battle of Copenhagen in 1801?
history.fact: According to the story, Nelson pretended not to see his commander's signal to withdraw and fought on.

history.q: Which Caribbean islands, now a US territory, did Denmark sell to the United States in 1917?
history.fact: The United States paid $25 million in gold for St Thomas, St John and St Croix.

history.q: Which country did Denmark have to give up to Sweden in 1814?
history.fact: Under the Treaty of Kiel, Denmark kept Norway's old Atlantic possessions: Greenland, Iceland and the Faroe Islands.

history.q: In October 1943, most of Denmark's Jews escaped Nazi deportation by crossing to which country?
history.fact: Fishermen and ordinary Danes ferried about 7,000 people across the Øresund in small boats.

history.q: Which Danish king built Copenhagen's Round Tower and Rosenborg Castle?
history.fact: Christian IV reigned from 1588 to 1648, the longest reign of any Danish monarch.

history.q: According to legend, the Danish flag fell from the sky during a 1219 battle in which present-day country?
history.fact: The Dannebrog is often cited as the oldest national flag still in continuous use.

history.q: In 1864, Denmark lost Schleswig and Holstein after a war against Prussia and which other power?
history.fact: The defeat at Dybbøl on 18 April 1864 remains a defining moment in Danish national memory.

history.q: After a 1920 plebiscite, which region returned from Germany to Denmark?
history.fact: The border drawn by that vote still stands, with a German minority to its north and a Danish minority to its south.

history.q: Which king, father of Harald Bluetooth, raised the smaller Jelling stone in memory of his wife Thyra?
history.fact: Gorm's inscription calls Thyra "Denmark's adornment", one of the earliest mentions of the name Denmark on Danish soil.

history.q: Which Danish king lost Skåne and other eastern provinces to Sweden in 1658?
history.fact: Frederick III used the crisis that followed to make himself an absolute monarch in 1660.

history.q: Ships paying Denmark's Sound Dues passed beneath which castle at Helsingør?
history.fact: Denmark charged ships sailing through the Øresund from 1429 until 1857, and the dues made the crown rich.

history.q: Which Danish Viking king conquered England in 1013?
history.fact: Sweyn died in early 1014 after only about five weeks as king; his son Cnut later won England back.

history.q: In 1792, Denmark became the first European country to decree a ban on which trade, effective from 1803?
history.fact: Slavery itself continued in the Danish West Indies until 1848, when it was abolished after an uprising.

history.q: Which Danish king rode alone on horseback through occupied Copenhagen as a symbol of national spirit?
history.fact: The popular story that he wore a yellow star in solidarity with Danish Jews is a legend, not fact.

history.q: Denmark's Kongeloven (Royal Law) of 1665 was a written constitution for what kind of rule?
history.fact: It was the only formal constitution of absolutism in Europe, and the king answered to God alone.

history.q: During which king's reign were Denmark's circular Viking ring fortresses, such as Trelleborg, built?
history.fact: Tree-ring dating places the building of Trelleborg around 980.

history.q: Which bishop is credited with founding Copenhagen in 1167?
history.fact: The ruins of Absalon's castle can still be seen beneath Christiansborg Palace.

history.q: Which Danish king was known as the "father-in-law of Europe"?
history.fact: His children included Queen Alexandra of Britain, Empress Maria Feodorovna of Russia and King George I of Greece.

history.q: In which year did Denmark officially adopt the Lutheran Reformation?
history.fact: Christian III seized the Church's lands after winning a civil war known as the Count's Feud.

history.q: Which medieval Danish historian wrote Gesta Danorum, which contains the Amleth story behind Hamlet?
history.fact: Saxo's tale of Amleth reached Shakespeare through later French retellings.

history.q: Which Danish king, nicknamed "Atterdag", reunited the kingdom and seized Visby on Gotland in 1361?
history.fact: His daughter Margaret went on to rule Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the Kalmar Union.

technology.q: In which Danish town was the LEGO company founded?
technology.fact: The name LEGO comes from the Danish words "leg godt", meaning "play well".

technology.q: Which Danish physicist won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the structure of atoms?
technology.fact: His son Aage Bohr also won the Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1975.

technology.q: Which Danish astronomer built the observatory of Uraniborg on the island of Hven?
technology.fact: Tycho lost part of his nose in a duel as a student and wore a metal replacement for the rest of his life.

technology.q: Which Danish brewery, founded in 1847, is known for the slogan "Probably the best beer in the world"?
technology.fact: Founder J.C. Jacobsen named it after his son Carl, and its laboratory isolated the first pure lager yeast in 1883.

technology.q: Which Danish shipping giant uses a white seven-pointed star on a blue background as its logo?
technology.fact: The company was founded in 1904 by Peter Mærsk Møller and his son A.P. Møller.

technology.q: Which Danish drugmaker makes Ozempic and Wegovy?
technology.fact: Its roots go back to 1923, when Nordisk began making insulin just after the hormone was discovered.

technology.q: Which Danish company is one of the world's biggest makers of wind turbines?
technology.fact: Vestas started as a blacksmith's shop in 1898 and built its first wind turbines in 1979.

technology.q: Which Danish physicist discovered in 1820 that an electric current can move a compass needle?
technology.fact: Ørsted's discovery linked electricity and magnetism, and in 1825 he also produced aluminium.

technology.q: Which Danish audio and TV brand is famous for its sleek modernist design?
technology.fact: Peter Bang and Svend Olufsen founded the company in 1925 in Struer, in western Jutland.

technology.q: Which Danish astronomer first showed that light has a finite speed, in 1676?
technology.fact: Rømer timed the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io and noticed they ran late when Jupiter was farther from Earth.

technology.q: Which Danish company's name combines "ventilation" and "lux", the Latin for light?
technology.fact: Engineer Villum Kann Rasmussen founded the roof-window maker in 1941.

technology.q: What did Danish engineer Valdemar Poulsen's 1898 "telegraphone" pioneer?
technology.fact: It recorded on steel wire; a recording of Emperor Franz Joseph made in 1900 is among the oldest surviving magnetic recordings.

technology.q: Danish computer scientist Bjarne Stroustrup created which programming language?
technology.fact: He began the work at Bell Labs in 1979, when the language was called "C with Classes".

technology.q: Greenland-born Danish-Canadian programmer Rasmus Lerdorf created which web language?
technology.fact: PHP originally stood for "Personal Home Page".

technology.q: The world's first offshore wind farm was built in 1991 off which Danish island?
technology.fact: The Vindeby farm's 11 turbines generated power for about 25 years before being taken down in 2017.

technology.q: Which interpretation of quantum mechanics is named after the city where Niels Bohr worked?
technology.fact: Bohr's institute in Copenhagen, opened in 1921, drew young physicists such as Werner Heisenberg and Wolfgang Pauli.

technology.q: Which Danish chemist introduced the pH scale in 1909?
technology.fact: He developed it at the Carlsberg Laboratory while studying the chemistry of proteins and brewing.

technology.q: Danish physician Niels Finsen won the 1903 Nobel Prize for treating disease with what?
technology.fact: Finsen used concentrated light to treat lupus vulgaris, a disfiguring skin form of tuberculosis.

technology.q: Which Danish company, founded in 1945 in Bjerringbro, is one of the world's largest pump makers?
technology.fact: Founder Poul Due Jensen started by building water pumps for farms in Jutland.

technology.q: Danish engineer Anders Hejlsberg was the lead architect of which Microsoft programming language?
technology.fact: He had earlier written Turbo Pascal and later co-designed TypeScript.

technology.q: Which Danish scientist won the 1920 Nobel Prize for discovering how capillaries regulate blood flow in muscles?
technology.fact: After visiting Canada, Krogh helped bring insulin production to Denmark, founding what became part of Novo Nordisk.

technology.q: Which vitamin did Danish biochemist Henrik Dam discover?
technology.fact: The K stands for "koagulation", because the vitamin is needed for blood to clot.

technology.q: Which Danish seismologist discovered in 1936 that the Earth has a solid inner core?
technology.fact: She worked it out from seismic waves of a 1929 New Zealand earthquake, and lived to the age of 104.

technology.q: Which engineering company did Mads Clausen found in his parents' farmhouse on the island of Als in 1933?
technology.fact: Danfoss, best known for valves, thermostats and drives, still has its headquarters at Nordborg on Als.

technology.q: Whose early temperature scale influenced Daniel Fahrenheit, who visited him in Copenhagen in 1708?
technology.fact: On Rømer's scale, water froze at 7.5 degrees and boiled at 60.

art.q: Which Danish author wrote "The Little Mermaid" and "The Ugly Duckling"?
art.fact: Andersen's fairy tales have been translated into more than 125 languages.

art.q: Which Danish architect designed the Sydney Opera House?
art.fact: Utzon left the project in 1966 and never saw the finished building in person.

art.q: Shakespeare's Hamlet is set at Elsinore, the castle known in Danish as what?
art.fact: Hamlet is often staged in the castle's courtyard; Laurence Olivier played the prince there in 1937.

art.q: Which Danish philosopher is often called the father of existentialism?
art.fact: Kierkegaard published many books under pseudonyms, including Either/Or (1843), signed "Victor Eremita".

art.q: Which Danish author wrote the memoir Out of Africa?
art.fact: She often wrote in English as Isak Dinesen, and her former farmhouse near Nairobi is now a museum.

art.q: Which Danish director made Breaking the Waves and Dancer in the Dark?
art.fact: Dancer in the Dark, starring Björk, won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 2000.

art.q: Which Danish actor played the Bond villain Le Chiffre in Casino Royale (2006)?
art.fact: Mikkelsen won Best Actor at Cannes in 2012 for the Danish drama The Hunt.

art.q: Which Danish-Norwegian pop group had a worldwide hit with "Barbie Girl" in 1997?
art.fact: Toy maker Mattel sued the band's record label over the song and lost.

art.q: Which Danish designer created the Egg and Swan chairs?
art.fact: He designed them for Copenhagen's SAS Royal Hotel, where he designed everything down to the cutlery.

art.q: Which Danish furniture designer created the Wishbone Chair?
art.fact: Wegner designed more than 500 chairs during his career.

art.q: Which Danish designer created the PH Artichoke lamp?
art.fact: Henningsen's layered shades were designed to give soft light without any glare from the bulb.

art.q: Which artists' colony gathered at a fishing village on Denmark's northern tip in the late 1800s?
art.fact: P.S. Krøyer's beach scenes captured the famous soft light of Skagen's summer evenings.

art.q: Which Danish painter is known for quiet grey interiors, often with a woman seen from behind?
art.fact: Many of his interiors show his own Copenhagen apartment at Strandgade 30.

art.q: Which Danish composer wrote six symphonies, including "The Inextinguishable"?
art.fact: Nielsen grew up on the island of Funen, and his portrait appeared on the 100-krone banknote.

art.q: Which Danish architect designed CopenHill, a waste-to-energy plant with a ski slope on its roof?
art.fact: The plant, opened in 2019, burns city waste to make electricity and heat for Copenhagen homes.

art.q: The Danish TV drama Borgen follows a woman who becomes what?
art.fact: "Borgen" ("The Castle") is the nickname for Christiansborg Palace, home of the Danish parliament.

art.q: Which Danish film, based on a Karen Blixen story, won the 1988 Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film?
art.fact: Bille August's Pelle the Conqueror won the same award a year later.

art.q: Which Danish-Icelandic artist installed a giant artificial sun in Tate Modern's Turbine Hall in 2003?
art.fact: The Weather Project drew about two million visitors, many of whom lay on the floor to gaze at the mirrored ceiling.

art.q: Which painter is called the father of Danish painting and led its Golden Age?
art.fact: Eckersberg studied in Paris under Jacques-Louis David before teaching a generation of Danish artists.

art.q: Which Danish neoclassical sculptor has a museum dedicated to his work beside Christiansborg Palace?
art.fact: Thorvaldsens Museum opened in 1848 as the first purpose-built museum building in Denmark.

art.q: Which Danish painter co-founded the avant-garde CoBrA movement in 1948?
art.fact: CoBrA took its name from the home cities of its founders: Copenhagen, Brussels and Amsterdam.

art.q: Which Danish novelist, author of Lucky Per, shared the 1917 Nobel Prize in Literature?
art.fact: Bille August turned Lucky Per into a film in 2018.

art.q: Which Danish poet structured her book-length poem "alphabet" on the Fibonacci sequence?
art.fact: Each section begins with a new letter, starting with apricot trees, and grows by the Fibonacci numbers.

art.q: Which Danish city's ARoS art museum is crowned by a circular rainbow-coloured walkway?
art.fact: Olafur Eliasson's "Your rainbow panorama" opened on the museum's roof in 2011.

art.q: Which director made Festen (The Celebration), the first film of the Dogme 95 movement?
art.fact: Festen won the Jury Prize at Cannes in 1998.
